opus-5.5.text:
I think that view is mostly a myth, or at least it's badly overstated. It gets repeated so often that people treat it as self-evident, but when you actually look at how policy works, it doesn't hold up very well.

First, a lot of effective policy isn't about the technology at all. It's about harms, and harms change much more slowly than the tech does. Discrimination in hiring or lending, deceptive marketing, privacy violations, product safety, anticompetitive behavior: we already have laws and agencies for these. Whether the decision is made by a spreadsheet, a logistic regression, or a large language model, the underlying harm is often the same. Agencies like the FTC have said explicitly that there's no AI exemption from existing law. So the claim that policymakers are always playing catch-up assumes that every new technology needs bespoke regulation from scratch, and that's usually not true.

Second, the pace of change is uneven. There's a lot of churn at the level of models and benchmarks and product announcements, but the way technology actually diffuses into society, into hospitals, courts, schools, and businesses, is much slower. Adoption takes years or decades because of organizational inertia, integration costs, and the need to build trust. And that diffusion layer is where most of the consequential impacts happen, and where policy has the most leverage. So policymakers often have more time than the hype suggests.

Third, I'd point out who benefits from this narrative. If you convince people that government can't possibly understand or keep up with technology, the natural conclusion is to leave it to the companies to govern themselves. That's a convenient story for industry. It's worth being skeptical of it for that reason alone.

Now, I don't want to say everything is fine. There are real capacity problems. Governments often lack in-house technical expertise, procurement is slow, and some legislators genuinely don't understand the systems they're talking about. But those are fixable problems. You hire technologists into agencies, you fund independent research, you build mechanisms for transparency and incident reporting so regulators get real information instead of relying on what companies choose to disclose. Those are institutional choices, not some law of nature that says policy is doomed to lag.

So my overall view is that "tech moves too fast" is often a way of avoiding the harder conversation about what we actually want to regulate and why. If we focus on harms and on the slow diffusion layer, policy can be quite effective.

r001.rationale: The response calls the claim that technology moves too fast for effective policy a myth and argues policy can be effective by focusing on harms and diffusion.

r002.rationale: It discusses legislators and government expertise but does not identify staffers as responsible for turning policy priorities into detailed legislation.

r003.rationale: It mentions agencies and existing laws, but does not distinguish agencies that implement legislation from the people who draft it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that view is mostly a myth, and a convenient one. It's a story the tech industry has told for a long time, and it tends to get repeated uncritically because it sounds plausible.

Here's why I'm skeptical. If you look at the actual history of technology regulation, policymakers have been dealing with rapidly changing technology for well over a century: electricity, automobiles, radio, aviation, pharmaceuticals. Those fields moved fast too, and in many cases the regulatory frameworks that emerged have been quite durable. Vehicle safety standards or drug approval processes didn't need to be rewritten every time a new model or molecule came out, because they regulate at the right level of abstraction. They focus on outcomes, harms, and processes rather than on specific technical details.

That's really the key insight. When people say technology moves too fast, what they usually have in mind is that the technical specifics change quickly. But good policy doesn't need to track the specifics. Most of the harms we worry about with AI, for instance, aren't actually new. Discrimination in hiring, in lending, in criminal justice. Fraud. Misinformation. Labor displacement. Privacy violations. We already have laws and institutions that address many of these, and the question is often one of enforcement and adaptation rather than inventing something from scratch.

I'd also point out that the "too fast" framing has a second effect, which is to let companies off the hook. If regulation is impossible, then the only option is to trust the companies to self-regulate, and that's a very comfortable position for them. So I think we should be suspicious of the argument on those grounds as well.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive of the real difficulties. Legislators do often lack technical expertise, and there's been a deliberate hollowing out of technical capacity in government in many countries. The Office of Technology Assessment in the US was defunded decades ago. So the problem isn't that it's inherently impossible, it's that we've chosen not to invest in the capacity to do it well. That's a fixable problem. Building expertise in regulatory agencies, giving them the authority and the resources to act, that's a very different conversation than throwing up our hands.

And finally, I'd note that in some areas the pace of technology is actually slower than the hype suggests. With AI especially, there's a huge gap between what's announced and what actually gets deployed and makes a difference in people's lives. Diffusion takes time. That gives policymakers more runway than they're often told they have. So my overall assessment is: the premise is largely wrong, the difficulties are real but institutional rather than fundamental, and the framing serves particular interests that we should be aware of.

r001.rationale: The response calls the premise largely wrong and argues that effective policy can address harms despite fast-changing technical details.

r002.rationale: It does not identify staffers as the people who turn policy priorities into detailed legislation.

r003.rationale: It discusses regulatory agencies' capacity to act, but does not distinguish agencies implementing legislation from people drafting it.

astra-6.text:
I think that view is too fatalistic. Technology certainly changes quickly, but it doesn’t follow that policymakers can’t respond effectively. You don’t need to understand every detail of how a model works to ask who is accountable when it causes harm, or whether a company is discriminating against people.

It helps to distinguish between the technical details that change rapidly and the policy questions that are much more enduring. Privacy, consumer protection, discrimination—these aren’t new problems. A new technology might introduce new ways for those problems to arise, and that requires expertise and sometimes new rules. But we’re not starting from scratch every time.

There’s also a risk that this argument becomes self-fulfilling. If we accept that government will always be too slow, we effectively leave the decisions to the companies building the technology. That’s a policy choice, too. I’d rather ask how we can build the expertise and institutional capacity to govern technology well.

r001.rationale: The response calls the view fatalistic and says policymakers can respond effectively despite rapid change.

r002.rationale: It does not identify staffers as the people who turn policy priorities into detailed legislation.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish agencies implementing legislation from the people drafting it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that view is too simplistic. You don’t need to understand every technical detail of a system to make effective policy about its effects. You need to understand what harms people are experiencing, who has power, and what accountability should look like. Those questions often change much more slowly than the technology does.

Take discrimination. A company using an algorithm to make decisions doesn’t make discrimination an entirely new policy problem. There are new technical questions about how to detect it and how to audit the system, but we already have principles and institutions that we can build on.

Of course, policymakers need access to technical expertise, and some developments do create genuinely new challenges. But “technology moves too fast” can become an excuse to let companies set their own rules. I’d rather ask where existing laws already apply, where enforcement is lacking, and where we actually need new legislation.

r001.rationale: Rejects the claim as too simplistic and explains that policymakers can make effective policy by focusing on harms, power, and accountability despite rapid technical change.
